title: How garbage collectors work: generations and G1
goal: By the end you can explain generations, copying and safepoints, say what write barriers and card tables are for, and read G1's young, concurrent and mixed collections in a real log.
opening:
The warehouse's cleaning crew has a problem of scale. The floor holds thousands of boxes, and checking every one of them on every round would take all day. So the crew looks hardest where the mess is. Near the door sit the new-arrivals shelves, and most boxes there are thrown out within minutes: packing, wrapping, delivery slips. Long-term storage hardly changes.

Java's garbage collectors are built on the same hunch. In the last lesson we saw which objects a collector may take away: everything the roots can't reach. This lesson watches it do the work, and the surprise is in the bill. A collector's work is measured by the objects it keeps, not by the garbage it throws away.

The easy trap is to treat the collector as a box with one dial, the heap size or the target pause time, and to turn it whenever the log looks bad. In this lesson, we'll see why the heap has generations and how a collector marks and moves objects. Then we'll watch G1 split the floor into regions and clean the messiest ones first. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: Two young collections each start with a full 500 MB eden. In the first, 5 MB of objects survive. In the second, 200 MB survive. Which pause is longer?
options: They take about the same time, because eden was the same size
The first, because it frees more memory
The second, because the collector copies every surviving object
Neither: young collections don't pause the application
warmup.why: A young collection copies the live objects out of eden and frees the rest in one go, so its cost follows the survivors, not the garbage. 200 MB of survivors is forty times the copying work. In G1, Serial and Parallel, young collections are stop-the-world pauses.

sections.h: Most boxes are thrown out young: why the heap has generations
sections.body:
A thumbnail request allocates a lot for a moment: the uploaded bytes, the decoded picture, the small thumbnail, a few strings and the response. All of it is garbage a few milliseconds later. A few objects live much longer: the cache of recent thumbnails, the service's settings, the map of uploads it has already done. That split has a name, the **weak generational hypothesis**: most objects die young.

The lesson's demo shows how lopsided it is. It runs a stand-in for the thumbnail service, with short-lived request objects and a slowly growing cache, and logs each young collection. In one JDK 25 run, the heap held 106 MB before a collection and 8 MB after it: 98 of the 106 MB were garbage.

HotSpot's collectors split the heap to match. New objects go into eden, the area where every object starts life. Eden belongs to the **young generation**, the new-arrivals shelves. When eden fills, a young collection finds the few live objects there and copies them into a survivor space, a small short-stay area. Everything else in eden is reclaimed at once, and the collector never even looks at it. Each time an object survives, its age goes up by one. The age lives in the 4 age bits of the mark word from lesson 1, the housekeeping strip on the label.

After enough survivals the object is **promoted**: copied into the **old generation**, long-term storage, which is collected much less often. The age at which that happens is the tenuring threshold. It's at most 15 (the `MaxTenuringThreshold` flag), and G1 lowers it when the survivor space runs short. The demo's age table, trimmed, shows both:

```text
GC(0) - age 1: 1755920 bytes
GC(1) - age 2: 1754832 bytes
GC(2) - age 3: 1754832 bytes
GC(3) Desired survivor size 8388608 bytes, new threshold 2 (max threshold 15)
GC(3) Old regions: 2->10
```

The same 1.75 MB of cache entries survived three collections, and its age went up by one each time. By GC(3) the survivors no longer fit the 8 MB of survivor space G1 wanted. So G1 dropped the threshold to 2, and everything that old went to long-term storage: the old generation grew from 2 regions to 10. (G1 counts its heap in regions, equal blocks of memory that a later section explains.)

Here the warehouse picture breaks, and the break is the key idea. A real crew leaves a wanted box where it is and carries out the rubbish. A copying collector does the opposite. It carries out every box it keeps, and then declares the whole area empty. That's why a young collection costs time in proportion to what survives, not to what was allocated, which was the warm-up.

It also makes medium-lived objects the expensive kind. They survive a few young collections, get copied each time, get promoted, and then die in the old generation, where only a bigger collection can reclaim them. A thumbnail cache whose entries live for ten minutes is exactly that shape.

Two questions follow. How does the crew find the boxes to keep? And how can it move a box while a worker is using it?

sections.h: Notes from old boxes to new ones: write barriers and card tables
sections.body:
There's a catch in the young collection story. To decide which young objects are alive, the collector follows references from the roots. But old objects point at young ones all the time: the thumbnail cache sits in the old generation, and every new entry it gets is a young object. If a young collection had to scan the whole old generation to find those pointers, it would cost as much as a full GC, a collection of the whole heap.

The fix is to do the bookkeeping at the moment the pointer is written. The heap is divided into **cards** of 512 bytes (G1 prints `CardTable entry size: 512` at start-up on JDK 25), and the **card table** has one byte per card. Every time your code stores a reference into a field, it also runs a few extra instructions, the **write barrier**, that mark the card holding that field as dirty. In the warehouse, it's a worker who writes a note inside a long-term box and also ticks that stretch of shelf on the floor plan:

```text
cache.entries[i] = thumbnail;                  // the store you wrote
card_table[address_of(field) >> 9] = DIRTY;    // what the barrier adds (512 = 2^9)
```

A young collection then scans the roots plus the dirty cards, not the whole old generation. G1 goes a step further. Each of its regions keeps a **remembered set**, the cards elsewhere in the heap that point into that region. "Merge Heap Roots" in G1's detailed pause log is the step that folds those remembered sets into the roots for the pause. (JDK 26 reworked how G1 processes the cards, in JEP 522; the barrier's job is the same.)

G1 has a second barrier, for concurrent marking: marking that runs while the program keeps going, which the last section of this lesson describes. While the program keeps running during marking, it can move a reference out of an object the marker hasn't visited yet into one it already has. To catch that, the barrier records the old value before a reference is overwritten, so the marker still finds every object that was live when marking began. The technique is called snapshot-at-the-beginning (SATB), and the comment on G1's barrier class in the JDK 25 source calls it "a logging barrier to support snapshot-at-the-beginning marking".

These barriers are the steady cost of a generational collector that works alongside your code: a few instructions on every reference store, all the time. Lesson 5 shows that ZGC, a collector built for very short pauses, pays at reference loads instead.

Reason it through before you move on. The service keeps a long-lived map of each user's latest thumbnail, so the map sits in the old generation. For every new thumbnail it replaces one user's value with the new, young object. Which cards does the barrier dirty, and what does the next young pause scan? (Only the few cards holding the map entries whose value changed. The pause scans those cards and the roots, finds the new thumbnails, and never reads the rest of the old generation.)

So far the heap has had fixed parts: eden, survivors, old. G1, the default collector, doesn't keep them fixed at all.

sections.h: G1 divides the floor into equal regions
sections.body:
**G1** (short for Garbage-First) is HotSpot's default collector. On JDK 25 it's the default on any machine with at least two processors and about 1.8 GB of memory, and from JDK 27 everywhere. G1 doesn't keep one big eden and one big old space. It cuts the heap into equal **regions**, and each region has a role for a while: eden, survivor, old, humongous or free. The roles move around. After a young pause the evacuated eden regions are free, and next time any of them can become anything. In the warehouse, G1's crew divides the floor into equal bays and labels each bay with its current use.

The region size comes from the maximum heap. In the JDK 25 source it's the max heap divided by 2048, held between 1 MB and 32 MB, then rounded up to a power of two. A 1 GB heap gets 1 MB regions, the 3.4 GB default heap on the machine behind this lesson got 2 MB, and `-Xmx40g` gets 32 MB.

Regions explain one of G1's sharp edges. An object larger than half a region is **humongous**. It skips TLABs (each thread's private chunk of eden, from lesson 2) and eden itself, and gets its own run of whole, contiguous regions, which count as old from the start. A 3 MiB photo in a `byte[]` is 3 MiB plus a 16-byte header, so with 1 MB regions it takes four regions, and nearly all of the fourth one is wasted. A burst of humongous allocations can start a concurrent marking cycle on its own (the next section's subject; the log gives the cause `G1 Humongous Allocation`), and each one needs enough free regions in a row. G1 does reclaim dead humongous objects early: in the demo on JDK 25, the first young pause freed `Humongous regions: 28->0`, seven dead photos at four regions each.

For the thumbnail service, the humongous objects are the photos themselves, whenever a whole upload sits in one array. If your log is full of `G1 Humongous Allocation`, stream those payloads instead of holding them whole (the compare block below shows how), or raise the region size with `-XX:G1HeapRegionSize` until they're under half a region.

G1 also works to a time budget. By default it aims to keep each pause under 200 ms (`MaxGCPauseMillis`), and it plans how much to collect in each pause to stay inside that budget. Regions are what make the plan possible: G1 can clean part of the old generation without cleaning all of it, and it cleans the messiest bays first, the way anyone tidies a garage with only an hour to spare.

To choose the messiest bays, though, G1 first has to know how much garbage each one holds.

sections.h: G1's cycle: young pauses, concurrent marking and mixed collections
sections.body:
Most of the time G1 runs only young pauses, and each one evacuates every eden and survivor region. Here's the first one from a JDK 25 run of the stand-in service, in a 256 MB heap:

```text
GC(0) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 28M->2M(214M) 12.921ms
```

Read it left to right. 28 MB was in use before, 2 MB after, the heap had 214 MB committed (memory the operating system has handed over; G1 grows it toward the 256 MB maximum as needed), and the stop-the-world pause took 12.9 ms on that busy 4-core machine. Your times will differ.

The old regions fill up slowly with promoted objects. When old-generation occupancy crosses the initiating heap occupancy percent (IHOP: 45% to begin with, then adapted from what G1 observes), G1 starts a **concurrent marking cycle**: an inspector who walks the long-term bays while work goes on, noting how full each one is. Here's one from the same run, with the timestamps cut off:

```text
GC(21) Pause Young (Concurrent Start) (G1 Humongous Allocation) 181M->127M(256M) 4.034ms
GC(22) Concurrent Mark Cycle
GC(22) Pause Remark 153M->153M(256M) 0.721ms
GC(22) Pause Cleanup 163M->163M(256M) 0.021ms
GC(22) Concurrent Mark Cycle 25.873ms
GC(23) Pause Young (Prepare Mixed) (G1 Evacuation Pause) (Evacuation Failure: Allocation) 253M->202M(256M) 4.001ms
GC(24) Pause Young (Mixed) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 242M->144M(256M) 3.110ms
```

The cycle starts inside a young pause (`Concurrent Start`). Marking then runs on a background thread for 26 ms while the program keeps working, with two short pauses to finish (`Remark`, `Cleanup`). Now G1 knows how much of each old region is live. The next young pause (`Prepare Mixed`) is the last young-only one. Then come the **mixed** pauses: all the young regions plus a few old ones, the ones with the most garbage. That choice is where the name Garbage-First comes from, and the mixed pause freed 98 MB where the young pause before it freed 51.

Which old regions? From the JDK 25 source: only regions less than 85% live are candidates (`G1MixedGCLiveThresholdPercent`). G1 sorts them by efficiency, best first. It drops the cheapest ones as long as the garbage it leaves behind stays within 5% of the heap (`G1HeapWastePercent`). And each mixed pause takes at least an eighth of the candidates, so the work is done in at most 8 mixed pauses (`G1MixedGCCountTarget`). The lab has you write these rules.

Two phrases in the log mean trouble. `(Evacuation Failure: Allocation)` means G1 ran out of free regions to copy into, and had to leave objects where they were. (JDK 21 printed only `(Evacuation Failure)`; newer JDKs add the reason.) `Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause)` is the fallback: the whole heap, mark-compact, every thread stopped. Both say the heap is too small for the live data plus the allocation rate.

It's tempting to lower `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis` to make them go away. The pause goal only steers how much work G1 plans per pause, such as how big eden gets and how many old regions a mixed pause takes. It can't create free regions, and a smaller goal usually means more, smaller pauses on the same full heap. **When G1 fails to copy, give it room or keep less alive. A smaller pause goal does neither.**

Here the warehouse picture breaks for the last time. A real crew can carry boxes while people work around them. G1 marks while the program runs, but it stops every thread before it moves anything, and that stop is your pause.

compare.title: Store an upload whole, or stream it

java.title: StoreUpload.java

kotlin.title: StoreUpload.kt

compare.note: The GC sees the same thing from both languages. The first version creates one array as big as the photo, which is humongous whenever the photo is over half a region, and the second never holds more than a small buffer. The difference is only in the API. Java's `transferTo` copies from an `InputStream` to an `OutputStream`, and the stream goes in try-with-resources. Kotlin's `copyTo` is an extension that does the same, and `use {}` closes the stream when the block ends. Making the thumbnail itself still needs the decoded picture, so streaming helps most where the program only moves bytes along.

steps.say: 1. Read the floor. The after-values (2, 7, 13, 28, 58, 88 MB) are what's still live after each young pause, and they climb by about 7 MB every pause. Either the service is warming a cache, or something is leaking. Either way the old generation is filling, and the committed heap grows from 214 MB toward its 256 MB maximum.

2. Find the turn. Two pauses later the heap is nearly full and copies start to fail. Humongous photos then start concurrent cycles. The first one that runs to the end tells G1 which old regions to clean, and the mixed pauses begin.
steps.code:
GC(14) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) (Evacuation Failure: Allocation) 234M->107M(256M) 16.851ms
GC(21) Pause Young (Concurrent Start) (G1 Humongous Allocation) 181M->127M(256M) 4.034ms
GC(22) Pause Remark 153M->153M(256M) 0.721ms
GC(22) Pause Cleanup 163M->163M(256M) 0.021ms
GC(23) Pause Young (Prepare Mixed) (G1 Evacuation Pause) (Evacuation Failure: Allocation) 253M->202M(256M) 4.001ms
GC(24) Pause Young (Mixed) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 242M->144M(256M) 3.110ms
GC(28) Pause Young (Mixed) (G1 Evacuation Pause) (Evacuation Failure: Allocation) 249M->156M(256M) 7.027ms

steps.say: 3. Read the verdict. The mixed pauses can't win. The first ones free about 95 MB each and later ones less and less (GC(40) freed 13 MB), and each time the heap is back near 250 MB a few milliseconds later. Then comes the fallback. The full GC brings the heap down to 95 MB, and that number is the live set at that moment: 95 MB of real data in a 256 MB heap, with a high allocation rate on top.

4. Decide. G1 copies, so it needs free regions to copy into. As a rule of thumb (mine, not G1's), give it a heap of two to three times the live set, and more when the live data swings, as it does here: this load's cache grows to 60% of the heap before it sheds half. Or keep less alive, by putting a limit on the cache. Then confirm with a new log that the evacuation failures and full GCs are gone. If the floor keeps climbing even then, it's a leak, not a sizing problem, and lesson 7 finds it.

lab.title: A toy collector, then G1 by numbers
steps: Run the tests. Fourteen of fifteen fail; the one that passes tests a helper you're given.

Start with the toy: write `ToyHeap.mark` without recursion. Keep an `ArrayDeque` of objects still to visit, take one off, mark it, and add its references. Then write `sweep`. The `ToyHeapTest` tests should pass, including the unreachable cycle and the 200,000-object chain.
Now G1. Write `regionSize`: divide by 2048, hold the result between 1 MB and 32 MB, then round up to a power of two. In that order. Each KDoc gives the rule from the JDK 25 source.
Write `isHumongous` (strictly more than half a region) and `regionsFor` (whole regions, rounded up).

Write `mixedCandidates`: filter, sort, then prune from the end, using the given `minOldRegionsPerMixedGc`. Run the tests until all fifteen pass, then read the test for the 3 MiB photo and explain its numbers to yourself.
hints: In `mark`, skip an object that is already marked when you take it off the deque. That one check ends cycles and avoids scanning anything twice.
`(a + b - 1) / b` rounds a division up, for positive numbers.
`coerceIn(MB, 32 * MB)` clamps. For the power of two, start at 1 MB and double until you reach the wanted size.
`compareByDescending { regionBytes - it.liveBytes }.thenBy { it.index }` sorts the candidates.
Pruning: walk back from the last candidate. Stop when you're down to the minimum, or when dropping the next one would push the total dropped garbage past 5% of the heap.

drill.title: Size G1's regions in your head
drill.prompt: Close the page. For a max heap of 6 GB: what region size does G1 pick? Is a 2.5 MB photo humongous there? How many regions does it take? Then write `regionSize` from memory.

recap: Most objects die young. A young collection copies the few survivors out of eden and frees the rest at once, so it costs what survives, not what was allocated. Survivors that age past the tenuring threshold are promoted to the old generation.
A collector marks what the roots can reach and frees the rest, so unreachable cycles go too. Copying costs what survives, and moving objects needs a stop-the-world pause at a safepoint.
Write barriers mark 512-byte cards dirty on every reference store, so a young collection scans dirty cards instead of the whole old generation. G1's SATB barrier keeps concurrent marking correct.
G1 cuts the heap into regions of 1 to 32 MB. Objects over half a region are humongous: they take whole contiguous regions and count as old from the start.

When old-generation occupancy crosses IHOP, G1 marks concurrently, then runs mixed pauses on old regions under 85% live, best first, in at most 8 pauses. `(Evacuation Failure: Allocation)` and `Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause)` mean the heap is too small for what's live, and the pause goal can't fix that.
The limit of G1: it marks alongside your code but stops every thread to move objects, so its pauses grow with the live objects each pause copies.
closing:
We started with a crew that looks hardest at the new-arrivals shelves, because most boxes there are thrown out young. G1 does the same with eden, copies the few survivors, tracks old-to-young notes with cards, and cleans the messiest old regions first, all while every thread waits.

Now find a GC log from a program of yours, or run one with `-Xlog:gc`. Read the number after the arrow on each young pause, and watch whether that floor climbs.

Next, we'll meet collectors that move boxes while the workers keep working: ZGC and Shenandoah. What does it cost to keep pauses under a millisecond, and how do you choose a collector?

quiz.q: A service runs on a 2 GB heap with G1 and default settings. Which of these is a humongous allocation?
options: `new byte[400_000]` for a thumbnail
A `HashMap` with 30,000 entries
`new byte[700_000]` for a chunk of an uploaded photo
A `String` of 300,000 Latin-1 characters
quiz.why: 2 GB / 2048 is exactly 1 MB, so regions are 1 MB and the humongous threshold is 512 KB. 700,000 bytes is over it. 400,000 bytes and a 300,000-character Latin-1 string (a 300 KB array) are under it. A `HashMap` is many small objects; with 30,000 entries its table has 65,536 slots, a 256 KB array.

quiz.q: Why does a young collection not have to scan the whole old generation for pointers into eden?
options: Old objects are never allowed to point to young objects
The write barrier marks dirty cards when references are stored, and the collector scans only those
The JIT moves such objects into the old generation right away
G1 copies the old generation in every young pause
quiz.why: Old-to-young pointers are normal, for example a cache in the old generation getting new entries. Every reference store runs a barrier that marks the 512-byte card it wrote to as dirty. A young pause scans the roots plus the dirty cards; in G1, remembered sets track which cards point into which region.

quiz.q: A JDK 25 log shows `GC(42) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 1210M->1180M(1536M)`, then `(Evacuation Failure: Allocation)` on the next pauses, then `Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 1490M->1150M(1536M)`. What does it tell you?
options: The pause goal is too high; set `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=50`
The young generation is too small; the old generation is fine
The application calls `System.gc()`
About 1.15 GB is really live in a 1.5 GB heap, which leaves G1 too little room to copy
quiz.why: The full GC's after-value is the live set: 1,150 MB of 1,536 MB. A young pause that frees only 30 MB, and copies that fail for lack of free regions, say the same thing. A smaller pause goal can't create free regions. A `System.gc()` call would show `(System.gc())` as the cause.

quiz.q: In `Safepoint "G1CollectForAllocation" ... Reaching safepoint: 48000000 ns, At safepoint: 2100000 ns ...`, where would you look first?
options: At the GC settings, because the collection took 48 ms
At application code that runs a long time without a safepoint check
At the heap size, because the heap is too small
At the number of GC worker threads
quiz.why: "Reaching safepoint" is the time the slowest thread took to stop: 48 ms here. The GC work itself, "At safepoint", took 2.1 ms. A long time to safepoint means some thread ran far without reaching a safepoint check, which no GC setting fixes.

quiz.q: From lesson 2: why is a dead 3 MiB photo cheaper for G1 than a 3 MiB photo that survives several young pauses, even though both are humongous?
options: A dead humongous object can be reclaimed in a young pause without any copying; a live one keeps its contiguous regions and fills the old generation
Live humongous objects are copied in every young pause
Dead humongous objects go into a TLAB
There is no difference; G1 treats all humongous objects alike
quiz.why: Humongous objects never go through TLABs or eden, and G1 doesn't copy them in young pauses. The demo showed a young pause freeing `Humongous regions: 28->0` because the photos were already dead. A live one keeps its regions as part of the old generation until it dies and a collection finds it.

flashcards.front: What does the weak generational hypothesis say?
flashcards.back: Most objects die young. Collectors use it by collecting a small young generation often and the old generation rarely.

flashcards.front: What does a young collection's pause time depend on?
flashcards.back: Mostly on how much survives and must be copied, not on how much garbage there is.

flashcards.front: What does a write barrier do in a generational collector?
flashcards.back: On every reference store, it marks the card (512 bytes in G1) that holds the field as dirty, so a young GC scans dirty cards instead of the whole old generation.

flashcards.front: How does G1 pick its region size by default?
flashcards.back: Max heap / 2048, held between 1 and 32 MB, rounded up to a power of two.

flashcards.front: When is an object humongous in G1?
flashcards.back: When it is bigger than half a region. It gets whole contiguous regions and skips TLABs and eden.

flashcards.front: Which old regions can a G1 mixed collection take?
flashcards.back: Regions under 85% live (`G1MixedGCLiveThresholdPercent`), best first, until the remaining garbage is within 5% of the heap.

flashcards.front: Two objects point at each other and nothing else points at them. Does a tracing GC free them?
flashcards.back: Yes. Marking only asks whether a root can reach an object, so an unreachable cycle is never marked and gets freed.

terms.plain: Eden plus survivor space, where new objects live until they die or are promoted.
Moving an object that survived enough young collections into the old generation.
G1's word for copying live objects out of a region so the region can be freed.
A moment when every application thread is stopped at a known place, so the GC can move objects.
One byte per 512-byte card of heap, marked dirty when a reference in that card changes.
G1's per-region list of cards elsewhere in the heap that point into the region.
In G1, an object bigger than half a region, stored in its own contiguous regions.
A G1 pause that evacuates the young regions plus some old regions with the most garbage.

explain_back.prompt: Explain to a new teammate, in your own words, what happens between G1's `Pause Young (Concurrent Start)` and its first `Pause Young (Mixed)`, and why G1 needs that step at all.
explain_back.answer: Young pauses only clean eden and survivor regions, so the old regions slowly fill with promoted objects. When old-generation occupancy crosses the IHOP threshold, the next young pause also starts a concurrent marking cycle. Marking runs on background threads while the application keeps going, and a write barrier records overwritten references so nothing live is missed. Two short pauses, Remark and Cleanup, finish it. Now G1 knows how much of each old region is live. After one more young-only pause (Prepare Mixed), the mixed pauses evacuate the young regions plus the old regions with the most garbage, at least an eighth of the candidates each time. Without marking, G1 couldn't know which old regions are worth copying, and the old generation would only be cleaned by a full GC.

deeper.body:
The `-Xlog:gc*` version of a young pause shows where the time goes. From a 1 GB heap on JDK 25:

```text
GC(2) Using 4 workers of 4 for evacuation
GC(2)   Pre Evacuate Collection Set: 0.07ms
GC(2)   Merge Heap Roots: 0.10ms
GC(2)   Evacuate Collection Set: 21.05ms
GC(2)   Post Evacuate Collection Set: 0.22ms
GC(2)   Other: 0.06ms
GC(2) Eden regions: 99->0(116)
GC(2) Survivor regions: 8->12(14)
GC(2) Old regions: 0->3
GC(2) Humongous regions: 4->0
GC(2) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 110M->14M(214M) 21.701ms
```

Almost all of the 21.7 ms is "Evacuate Collection Set", the copying. "Merge Heap Roots" is the remembered-set work from section 3, tiny here. `Eden regions: 99->0(116)` means 99 eden regions before, none after, and a target of 116 for the next cycle: G1 resizes eden after every pause to meet its pause goal. `Old regions: 0->3` means three regions' worth of survivors were promoted, and `Humongous regions: 4->0` is one dead 3 MiB photo reclaimed without copying.

The G1 defaults behind this lesson, from the JDK 25 source: `InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent` 45 with `G1UseAdaptiveIHOP` on, `G1MixedGCCountTarget` 8, `G1HeapWastePercent` 5, `G1MixedGCLiveThresholdPercent` 85 (an experimental flag), `G1ReservePercent` 10 (free space G1 tries to keep for copying), and `MaxTenuringThreshold` 15. `MaxGCPauseMillis` is 200 when G1 is the collector.

One more line you'll meet: `Concurrent Undo Cycle`. It appears when a humongous allocation asked for a concurrent start, but by the time marking would begin, occupancy was back under the threshold, so G1 abandoned the cycle. That reading comes from the logs, not from G1's documentation.
